# Semantic-Anchored Checkpointing for Stateless Agent Seats

## 0. The core invariant everything hangs on

Causal attention means KV at position *i* depends only on tokens `[0, i]`. Therefore:

> **KV for `[0, p)` is reusable iff tokens `[0, p)` are provably unchanged.**

Everything below is machinery to make "provably unchanged" cheap to establish after a death/respawn, and to make edits land *exactly* on positions where a checkpoint exists. Semantic anchors are that alignment device: **the edit grammar is restricted to anchor-aligned operations**, so the first-modified-position of any edit is always a signed checkpoint.

---

## 1. Data model

### Segments (unit of provenance *and* cache reuse)

```text
Segment := {
  seg_id:  H(token_ids)          // content-addressed
  n_tok:   u32                   // ≤ 256
  role:    SYS|USER|ASSISTANT|TOOL|SUMMARY|STUB
  cites:   [seg_id]              // mandatory for SUMMARY/STUB
}
CtxVersion := [seg_id]*          // ordered; ctx_root = verkle root over {idx → seg_id}
```

Segments are capped at 256 tokens. Every segment boundary is an anchor candidate. An edit is any operation producing a new `CtxVersion` sharing a prefix with the old one; the first divergent index gives the invalidation point.

### Anchor (the checkpoint)

```text
Anchor := {
  anchor_id, parent: H(prev anchor)
  ctx_root:    H                  // verkle root over segment list
  tok_offset:  u64                // Σ n_tok — cumulative token position
  kv_root:     H                  // verkle root over {(page_span) → H(kv_bytes)}
  kv_fmt:      {model_id, dtype=f16, kernel_class}
  imm_end:     u32                // immutable-zone boundary (see §2)
  tag:         TURN_END|TOOL_RESULT|SUMMARY|PERIODIC|PROMOTION|TAIL
  sampler:     {cfg_hash, seed_commit}
  gate_sig:    BLS(k-of-3)
}
```

`kv_root` maps `(page_span_idx → content hash)` where a page span is 256 tokens × all layers/heads. **Key layout: stem = `H(span_idx)`, suffix = `(layer, kv_head)`** — one verkle proof covers all 640 entries (L=80, GQA 8) of a span. Page bytes live in a CAS keyed by *their own content hash*, so `kv_root` binds position→hash and the CAS stores bytes→bytes. Consequence: a fetched page either matches its committed hash exactly or the fetch failed. **Corruption reduces to unavailability.** There is no poisoning attack to defend against, only misses.

### Edit transactions

```text
EditTx := {
  base_ctx_root: H,              // CAS-style guard; stale ops rejected
  op: APPEND(segs) | SPLICE(i, segs) | EVICT(i..j) | PROMOTE(i..j),
  actor, policy_lease,
  expected_first_invalid: u64    // gate recomputes and compares
}
Receipt := {edit_id, new_ctx_root, first_invalid_offset, gate_sig}
```

The gate enforces: authorization (actor vs. region ACL), budget (zone caps), schema (`cites` non-empty on summaries), and that `first_invalid_offset` equals `tok_offset` of segment `i` — i.e., **the invalidation point is a signed anchor or the tx is rejected.** This is the load-bearing rule tying edits to checkpoints.

---

## 2. Two-zone context (this is what makes eviction affordable)

Naive eviction of ancient history invalidates everything downstream and forces massive re-prefill. Solve it structurally:

- **Immutable zone** `[0, imm_end)`: system prompt, constitution, promoted long-term memory. Never edited in place. KV pinned hot in every seat's NVMe, content-deduped across sessions (same system prompt ⇒ same page hashes ⇒ free sharing). Bounded: ≤ 8k tokens.
- **Mutable zone** `[imm_end, end)`: working context, ≤ 32k tokens. All splices/evictions/summaries happen here. Worst-case re-prefill = mutable-zone length ≈ 32k tokens ≈ 3 s at ~10k tok/s prefill. Typical case (edit near tail): < 1k tokens, < 0.1 s.

`PROMOTE(i..j)` graduates mutable segments into the immutable zone: one bounded re-prefill of the immutable zone, paid rarely, recorded as its own anchor tagged `PROMOTION`.

---

## 3. What persists vs. recomputes

| Artifact | Location | Lifetime | On respawn |
|---|---|---|---|
| Header chain + quorum checkpoints | chain | forever | verify 1 checkpoint sig + K headers |
| Anchor records (ctx_root, tok_offset, kv_root, tag, seed) | chain | forever | read last finalized |
| Edit txs + gate receipts | chain | forever | audit replay only |
| Segment bodies (token ids) | CAS | forever | fetch + hash-verify |
| **KV page tensors** | hot NVMe → warm CAS → **nothing** | minutes → days → ∞ | fetch+verify, else **re-prefill** |
| Sampler config, seeds | anchor record | forever | read |
| RoPE tables, attention page tables | — | ephemeral | derive |
| Decode-loop state, uncommitted tail KV | volatile | dies with seat | regenerate from last anchor/receipt |
| Chat-template rendering | — | ephemeral | render from `template_ver` pinned at session genesis |

The principle: **commitments persist forever; tensors persist per availability tier; recompute is the universal fallback and is always safe because the token log is the root of trust.** KV is a derived artifact. The chain never stores a float.

Tail loss bounding: decode flushes a signed **tail receipt** every 256 tokens or 500 ms (`{prev_receipt, H(new tokens), running_offset, sig}`). Receipts extend the context past the last anchor; their KV is uncommitted, so respawn re-prefills ≤ ~300 tokens of tail. Seed is committed in the anchor ⇒ regeneration is bit-deterministic if audit demands it.

---

reasoning:
The user is asking about a hard systems design problem: semantic-anchor checkpoints for an agent's context editing system, where context edits re-prefill only the new suffix, integrated with a verkle chain / provenance gate. The design must work for a "stateless seat" — an agent process that dies and respawns, so we need to be precise about what persists vs. what recomputes.

Let me think about this deeply.

**Context of the problem:**

Modern LLM agents have a KV cache from prefilling a prompt. When the agent's context is edited (e.g., tool results appended, old turns evicted/summarized, memory compaction), naive systems re-prefill the whole context. The optimization: if an edit only appends or modifies a suffix, you can reuse the KV cache prefix and re-prefill only the new suffix. This is prefix caching / incremental prefill.

But there's a problem: **provenance and integrity**. If the seat is stateless (dies, respawns on another machine), how do we know that:
1. The KV cache prefix it's about to reuse actually corresponds to the claimed token prefix?
2. The edit was legitimate (authorized by the provenance gate)?
3. The semantic anchors (checkpoints) are valid?

**Verkle chains**: Verkle trees allow small proofs (polylogarithmic in state size) with vector commitments. A verkle chain would be a blockchain-like structure where each block commits to a state root via a verkle tree. Provenance gate = the component that verifies that any piece of state (context, anchors, KV commitments) has a valid proof chain back to genesis or a trusted root.

**Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: Instead of anchoring at token boundaries only, anchor at *semantic* boundaries — e.g., after a completed reasoning step, after a tool call result is ingested, at turn boundaries, at summary boundaries. Each anchor records:
- The exact token prefix hash (or merkle/verkle path) up to that point
- The KV cache commitment (a Merkle/verkle root over per-layer, per-head K/V blocks)
- Semantic metadata (what the anchor means: "post-tool-result", "post-summary", etc.)
- Signature/witness from the provenance gate

When an edit happens:
- If the edit touches only positions ≥ anchor N, then all KV blocks before anchor N are reusable; re-prefill from anchor N.
- If the edit is a suffix append, trivially reuse everything.
- If the edit modifies mid-context (e.g., replaces a span), find the deepest anchor below the first modified position; discard KV from there onward; re-prefill the suffix.

**Stateless seat**: The agent process holds no durable state. It dies and respawns. So:

What persists (in the verkle chain / external storage):
- The anchor ledger: sequence of anchors with their commitments
- The raw token log (or its commitments + content-addressed blobs)
- The KV cache blocks themselves? Or just their commitments?

Key design decision: persisting actual KV tensors is expensive. Options:
1. Persist KV blocks to a content-addressed store (e.g., keyed by hash of (layer, head, block index, token range)), with commitments in the verkle tree. On respawn, fetch blocks by proof.
2. Recompute KV from tokens on respawn (prefill cost).
3. Hybrid: hot tier keeps recent KV; cold tier recomputes.

For a truly stateless seat, the honest answer: **the canonical persistent artifact is the token log + anchor ledger in the verkle chain; KV cache is a derived, reconstructible artifact whose integrity is guaranteed by commitments but whose availability is best-effort.**

So what persists vs recomputes:

**Persists (verkle chain + blob store):**
1. Token log segments (content-addressed chunks, e.g., 4k-token pages). Committed as leaves in the verkle tree.
2. Anchor records: {anchor_id, seq_no, token_position, tokenizer_version, model_id, kv_root, semantics_tag, parent_anchor, edit_witness}. These are transactions in the chain.
3. Edit records: every context mutation is a transaction: {edit_id, base_anchor, op (append/splice/evict/rewrite), payload_ref or inline bytes, resulting_anchor}.
4. KV block commitments: for each anchor, a verkle root over the set of KV blocks {(layer, head, block_idx) → H(kv_bytes)}. Optionally the blocks themselves in a CAS with availability SLA.
5. Policy/provenance attestations: who authorized each edit, gate verdicts.

**Recomputes (on respawn):**
1. Tokenization verification: re-derive token ids from stored text? No — store token ids directly (tokenizer pinned by version); verify by hashing.
2. KV cache: either fetch blocks verified against kv_root (fast path) or recompute prefill from the nearest anchor (slow path). Never trust unverified local disk.
3. Position embeddings / RoPE offsets: deterministic from token positions; recompute.
4. Sampling state: RNG seed committed in anchor record; recompute deterministically.
5. In-flight partial decode: lost; the last committed anchor defines the recovery point. Any tokens generated after the last anchor commit are discarded or re-committed via a "tail witness" mechanism.

Wait — there's a subtlety: decode steps generate tokens one at a time. Do we commit an anchor per token? That's too much overhead. Design: commit anchors at semantic boundaries only; between anchors, the seat may hold uncommitted tail state. If the seat dies mid-decode, the tail is lost and regeneration resumes from last anchor. To bound loss, define max-tail-length policy: force an anchor commit every N generated tokens (N ~ 256–1024) or at tool-call boundaries (mandatory).

Actually, let me reconsider: "semantic-anchor checkpoints" — the checkpoints are at semantic boundaries. The re-prefill-only-suffix property requires that when an edit invalidates part of the context, we can resume from the deepest valid anchor. Anchors must therefore be frequent enough that suffix re-prefill is cheap, but semantic enough that they're stable under edits.

There's tension: anchors inside a "thought" are semantically unstable (an edit upstream changes meaning downstream even if tokens are identical? No — actually for transformer KV cache, if tokens are identical, KV is identical regardless of semantics. Semantics matter for *correctness of reuse across edits*: if an edit changes earlier text, downstream KV is stale even if downstream tokens unchanged, because attention depends on prior keys/values. So the rule is purely positional: KV for positions < first_modified_position is reusable; positions ≥ are not. Semantic anchors are a way to choose *where* to place resumable boundaries such that typical edits invalidate from a boundary.)

Hmm, but there's a deeper subtlety: attention is causal, so KV[i] depends only on tokens ≤ i. Therefore KV prefix reuse validity is exactly: tokens[0..p) unchanged ⇒ KV[0..p) reusable. Edits that splice at position p invalidate KV[p..end]. So the checkpoint granularity question is purely about where edits tend to land vs where anchors are. Semantic anchors placed at: end of user turn, end of assistant turn, end of tool result ingestion, start/end of summarized regions, memory-block boundaries. Edits (compaction, summarization, eviction) are designed to land on these boundaries. That's the co-design: the editor only performs operations aligned to anchors, so invalidation always starts exactly at an anchor.

That's the key insight to make concrete: **the edit grammar is restricted to anchor-aligned ops**, so the "first modified position" is always an anchor position. Then suffix re-prefill starts from that anchor's KV commitment.

Now the verkle chain integration:

Why verkle rather than merkle? Because we need efficient proofs of individual KV blocks and token pages without revealing the whole tree, and witness size matters when the seat is stateless and must fetch proofs over the network. Verkle gives O(log n)-ish (actually polylog with small constant, ~ hundreds of bytes per proof with IPA-based schemes) proofs. Also verkle supports efficient insertion into large key-value state (like Ethereum's state tree plans): each anchor extends the state; the state root after each edit is committed in a block header. The "chain" part: each block contains {prev_hash, state_root (verkle root), edit_txs, anchor_txs, timestamp, signer}.

Provenance gate: a service (or smart-contract-like verifier) that:
- Validates each edit tx against policy (who may edit which region, budget limits, schema checks)
- Computes the new state root
- Issues a signed receipt: {edit_id, base_state_root, new_state_root, anchor_id}
The seat cannot self-certify edits; the gate's signature on the anchor record is what makes a checkpoint trustworthy. On respawn, the seat presents the gate receipt chain (or fetches it) and verifies signatures against the gate's public key pinned in the genesis config.

KV cache integrity without storing tensors in-chain: 
- kv_root at anchor A = verkle root over map {(layer l, head h, page p) → H(bytes)} for all positions < A.pos.
- Pages are fixed-size token spans (e.g., 128 tokens × 32 layers... actually per layer per head per page). Key = H(model_id || layer || head || page_index || anchor_pos?) Hmm — careful: KV values depend on the full prefix, but for a given token position they're deterministic given tokens[0..pos]. Since anchors pin the token log, page content is deterministic: key = H(model_id, tokenizer_ver, layer, head, page_start_token_index). Content-addressed. Deterministic given the token prefix — yes because causal attention: KV at position i depends only on tokens ≤ i. So the same token prefix always yields the same KV bytes (modulo nondeterminism in GPU kernels!).

Ah — nondeterminism: floating-point reduction order varies across GPUs/batches, so recomputed KV won't be bit-identical. Two options:
(a) Commit to *canonicalized* KV: quantize to fp16/bf16 with deterministic rounding, or store fp32 with defined rounding; require producers to run in deterministic mode (fixed batch size 1 prefill, deterministic kernels). Expensive but doable.
(b) Commit to a tolerance: verify fetched KV by spot-checking against recomputed values within epsilon. Weaker provenance.
(c) Don't commit KV bytes at all; commit only the token log, and treat KV as pure cache (recompute on miss). Provenance gate then only guards the *token/context* lineage, not tensor bits.

Honest engineering answer: (c) for correctness-critical path, with (a) as an optional fast-path integrity check. Actually let me think again. The point of committing kv_root is to let a respawned seat *reuse* cached tensors without trusting the cache host. If we don't commit KV, then any reused KV is trusted-but-unverified, and a malicious/buggy cache could poison generation while the provenance gate says everything's fine. For a "provenance gate" to mean anything, KV reuse must be gated too. So: commit kv_root with deterministic-KV requirement (option a), and define the fallback: if a fetched page fails verification (hash mismatch), discard and recompute from the deepest verified anchor. Verification of a page = verkle proof against kv_root + hash match. That's cheap (no recompute needed to verify a hash!). Right — verifying fetched KV is just hash checking against the committed root; no floating point involved. The determinism issue only arises if we want to *recompute* and compare. So: fast path = fetch + hash-verify against kv_root (bit-exact required from producer at write time; producer computes KV once, hashes, commits — no cross-machine reproducibility needed!). 

That resolves the nondeterminism concern elegantly: the kv_root is computed by whichever seat produced the KV originally; consumers verify hashes, never recompute-and-compare. Recompute happens only on cache miss, and the recomputed KV becomes the new committed truth only if... hmm, wait: if seat B recomputes KV for the same token prefix and gets different bits than seat A's committed root, B can't use its own recomputation without violating the committed root. Fix: recompute → hash → if matches committed root, fine; if not, the seat must either (i) write a "kv amendment" tx recording the new root (with justification "kernel-version change"), gated like any edit, or (ii) treat mismatch as corruption and fall back further. Simpler: make the kv_root keyed by kernel/build version: kv_root = root over pages produced by build X; a respawned seat with build Y recomputes under Y and writes a fresh anchor with kv_root_Y referencing the same token position. The anchor record includes {model_build, attn_kernel_ver}; equivalence classes of builds that are bit-compatible share roots. This is getting deep but it's the real engineering.

Simplify for the answer: include `kv_format_id` (model id, dtype, kernel determinism class) in the page key. Mismatch ⇒ recompute locally and register a new anchor variant; the chain keeps both, provenance intact.

Now, the respawn flow, concretely:

Seat S dies at time T with last committed anchor A_k (position p_k, kv_root R_k). Uncommitted tail: tokens p_k..p_now possibly partially decoded — lost, unless a "tail flush" happened. Add mechanism: the seat streams generated tokens to the log-append service with periodic soft commits (every M tokens or T_ms); soft commits become anchors only after gate signature. Death window loss ≤ M tokens / T_ms.

Respawn:
1. Fetch latest gate-signed head: (state_root, last_anchor_id). Verify chain of headers back to pinned genesis (or a recent checkpoint signed by k-of-n gate quorum — otherwise replay cost grows).
2. Reconstruct context view: read token pages for [0, p_k) — either full log or, if compaction happened, the *materialized view* defined by the edit history. Important: compaction edits rewrite the logical context; the logical context is itself a verkle-map: ctx_root over {slot → content_ref}. Anchors reference ctx_root, not raw positions? Let me think.

Two models:
- **Append-only log model**: context is a log; edits are appends plus tombstones/summaries that replace ranges. Logical position = log index. Compaction = replace range [a,b) with summary token span; this is a splice at a, invalidating KV[a..end). All subsequent anchors re-stamped.
- **Slot-map model**: context is a map slot→block; edits update slots; "prefix reuse" is murkier because slot order defines token order; changing slot contents shifts positions.

Append-only-with-splices is cleaner for KV reuse. Define the materialized context as a sequence of segments; each segment immutable, content-addressed; context version = list of segment refs. An edit produces a new segment list sharing a prefix with the old. First-divergent-index d = length of shared prefix. KV reusable iff segments[0..d) byte-identical AND their token spans identical ⇒ reuse KV up to cumulative token count D(d). Anchors are stamped at segment boundaries with cumulative token offset. Deepest anchor with offset ≤ D is the resume point. This generalizes splices naturally: any edit's invalidation point is a segment boundary if we require edits to operate on whole segments (anchor-aligned ops). Good — formalize: **edits are segment-granular; segments are the unit of both provenance and cache reuse.**

3. KV acquisition: for pages [0, P_resume): try CAS fetch by key; verify verkle proof against R_k (per-anchor roots make proofs small: prove membership of page keys in the anchor's kv subtree). Missing/corrupt pages ⇒ mark gap; recompute gap by prefilling the token span of the gap (needs left neighbor KV as context — prefill from the previous contiguous verified page boundary). Worst case: full re-prefill from 0. Expected case: hot pages present, zero recompute.
4. Resume generation at p_k (+ flushed tail if recovered from log-append service with its own receipts — the tail flush should also be gate-receipted so it's trustworthy; call these micro-anchors or "tail receipts").

Cost accounting (be concrete):
- Persist per anchor: ~200–500 B record + verkle witness updates. At 1 anchor/512 tokens, a 1M-token session ≈ 2k anchors ≈ ~1 MB of chain data. Fine.
- KV footprint: e.g., 70B-class model, GQA 8 kv heads, head_dim 128, fp16: per token per layer = 8×128×2×2 B = 4 KB; ×80 layers = 320 KB/token?? That's huge — 1M tokens = 320 GB. Realistic sessions are shorter; still, KV persistence is the dominant cost. Hence tiering: keep KV pages for last W tokens (W ~ 64–256k) in warm CAS; older pages dropped, recoverable only by recompute. The chain keeps commitments regardless (cheap); availability is tiered. State this explicitly: **commitments persist forever; tensors persist per-tier SLA; recompute is the universal fallback.**
- Re-prefill cost: suffix-only prefill from anchor at ~ (suffix_tokens) × prefill FLOPs; with 8×A100-ish throughput numbers maybe skip hardware specifics, give formula: t_prefill ≈ N_suffix / r_prefill where r_prefill is tokens/sec for the deployment; reuse saves (1 − p_resume/p_total) of prefill compute.

Edit grammar (concrete ops):
1. APPEND(segment): new segment at tail; invalidates nothing; new anchor optional (auto-anchor at segment close).
2. SPLICE(seg_ref → replacement segments): allowed only if seg_ref is anchor-aligned (segment start == some anchor offset). Invalidates KV from that offset. Gate checks: replacement token budget, policy tags preserved.
3. EVICT(range of segments): replace with stub token ("[evicted: ref]") or nothing; invalidates from first evicted offset.
4. REWRITE_META: annotations outside token stream; no invalidation.
5. COMPACT: composite op = EVICT + APPEND(summary); lands on anchors by construction.

Gate checks per op: authorization (editor identity vs ACL on region), budget (context length caps), schema (summary must cite source segment refs — provenance links), non-regression (new ctx_root ≠ old, monotone version). Receipt: {op_id, base_ctx_root, new_ctx_root, first_invalid_offset, gate_sig}.

Anchor record fields (exact):
```
Anchor {
  anchor_id: u64            // monotone
  parent: anchor_id
  ctx_root: H               // verkle root over segment list
  tok_offset: u64           // cumulative token count at this boundary
  kv_root: H                // verkle root over {(l,h,page)->H(bytes)} for tokens < tok_offset
  kv_format: {model_id, dtype, kernel_class}
  tag: enum {TURN_END, TOOL_RESULT, SUMMARY_BOUNDARY, PERIODIC, TAIL_FLUSH}
  gen_state: {rng_seed_commit, sampler_cfg_hash}
  gate_sig
}
```

What persists vs recomputes — final crisp table:

Persists (durable, in chain/CAS):
- Segment blobs (token ids + text) — forever (or until GC policy with re-derivation from summaries? No: keep forever; they're small relative to KV).
- Edit txs + gate receipts — forever.
- Anchor records incl. kv_roots — forever.
- Header chain — forever (with periodic quorum checkpoints to bound verification).
- KV tensors — tiered: hot (NVMe/local, minutes), warm (CAS, hours–days), cold (none; recompute). Commitments forever.
- Sampler config, seeds — forever (tiny).

Recomputes (ephemeral, per-seat-lifetime):
- KV pages not found in warm/hot tiers — via prefill from deepest contiguous verified page boundary.
- RoPE tables, position offsets — trivially derived.
- Attention metadata (page tables, block maps) — rebuilt from anchor + fetched pages.
- Decoding loop state (last logits, beam state if any) — restart from last anchor/tail receipt; sample afresh with committed seed ⇒ deterministic regeneration of the lost tail if desired (seed committed ⇒ same tokens regenerated, then re-commit).
- Tokenizer caches, chat-template rendering — derived from pinned template version; template version must be part of ctx_root derivation (template change = global invalidation; pin it).

Edge cases to nail:
- Template/tokenizer upgrade mid-session: forbid; version pinned in session genesis; upgrades start a new session with migration tx (old ctx_root referenced, new prefill from scratch, provenance link recorded).
- Concurrent editors: gate serializes via per-session sequencer; ops carry base_ctx_root; CAS-style compare-and-swap on ctx_root rejects stale ops.
- Fork/reorg of the chain: seats pin genesis + follow heaviest chain; anchors are final after quorum checkpoint depth D_f; seats may optimistically use unconfirmed anchors but must re-verify after finality; on reorg, roll back to last finalized anchor and re-prefill the delta. Give D_f concretely, e.g., finalize every 32 blocks / 10 s.
- Cache poisoning attack: adversary serves wrong KV bytes with valid-looking proof? Impossible if hash doesn't match committed root — verkle proof binds key→value-hash; serving different bytes fails hash check. Serving correct-hash bytes for wrong key (key confusion): keys include model/kernel/page-index, so cross-contamination needs hash collision. Fine.
- Rollback of an edit (undo): undo is a new forward edit (splice back original segment refs); invalidation computed the same way. Chain never rewrites history.
- Tail receipts during decode: micro-commit every M=256 tokens or 500 ms, whichever first; receipt = {session, prev_receipt, H(new tokens), running tok_offset, sig}. On respawn, tail receipts extend context beyond last anchor; their KV isn't committed, so re-prefill the tail (≤ M+latency tokens) — bounded small.

Verification cost on respawn: verify header chain to last quorum checkpoint (~1 header per block; with 1 block/edit-batch, thousands of headers — use quorum-signed checkpoints every K blocks so respawn verifies O(K) headers + 1 checkpoint sig). Then verify: last anchor sig, ctx_root membership proofs for each segment ref (one verkle proof per segment, ~few hundred bytes each), KV page proofs per fetched page. Total for 100-segment, 2000-page restore: ~2100 proofs × ~300 B ≈ 630 KB network + ms-scale CPU. Concrete.

Failure containment: if gate unavailable, seat may continue in "optimistic mode": edits buffered locally, anchors unsigned; on gate return, batch-submit; until then, respawn cannot trust optimistic anchors — recovery point = last gate-signed anchor. Tradeoff stated plainly.

Also address: why semantic anchors specifically (vs every-N-tokens)? Because (1) edit ops are defined at semantic boundaries so invalidation aligns exactly, (2) anchors double as audit points for the provenance gate (tool results, summaries get individual accountability), (3) kv_root per anchor lets proofs be scoped small. Periodic anchors (PERIODIC tag) cap worst-case suffix length between semantic ones.

I should also give the invariant set formally:
- I1 (Prefix soundness): KV page for token range [a,b) usable iff there exists a gate-signed anchor A with A.tok_offset ≥ b and the token log [0,b) hashes to the values committed under A.ctx_root lineage.
- I2 (Invalidation): after edit with first_invalid_offset f, all anchors with tok_offset > f are stale for generation; resume anchor = max anchor with tok_offset ≤ f.
- I3 (Determinism binding): generation claims (outputs) cite anchor_id + sampler seed; auditors can reproduce given persisted segments + config.
- I4 (No silent mutation): every byte of logical context traceable to an edit tx signed by gate; ctx_root chain is hash-linked.

Implementation sketch: name concrete components — Log Append Service (LAS), CAS (content-addressed store, e.g., keyed by SHA-256), Gate (signing service, HSM-backed keys, quorum k=3of5), Seat runtime (fetcher, verifier, prefill worker, decode loop). Maybe give pseudo-code for respawn() and apply_edit(). Keep tight.

Numbers: pick a concrete model shape for examples: L=80 layers, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, fp16 → KV bytes/token = 80×8×128×2×2 = 327,680 B ≈ 320 KiB/token. Page = 256 tokens → 80 MiB/page. Hmm that's big; page per (layer,head) instead: page = (layer, head, 256 tokens) = 256×128×2×2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB. Number of pages per 256-token span = 80×8=640. So per anchor covering 256 new tokens: 640 new pages, 80 MiB total. Warm-tier for last 64k tokens: 20 GiB. That's plausible for a node. Cold: recompute. Good, use these numbers.

Prefill rate assumption: ~5–20k tok/s on a big-GPU node for a 70B model (roughly realistic for prefill-bound, e.g., ~10k tok/s). Suffix re-prefill of 4k tokens ≈ 0.4 s. Full 100k re-prefill ≈ 10 s.
